lead: An LTI system can be described by how it treats each frequency. If x(t) has Fourier transform X(ω), the output has Y(ω)=H(ω)X(ω). The complex number H(ω) is the frequency response. It scales amplitude by |H(ω)| and shifts phase by ∠H(ω). This turns time-domain convolution into multiplication in frequency. Engineers use it to read RC filters, audio tone controls, communication channels and control loops. The same idea explains why a bass note and a treble note leave a filter with different strengths and delays.
prereq: You need: 3.2 and 3.3; Unit 2 impulse response and convolution.

blocks.text: For an LTI system with impulse response h(t), the frequency response is the Fourier transform of h(t).

blocks.where: H(ω) is the complex frequency response; Y(ω) and X(ω) are Fourier transforms of output y(t) and input x(t); h(t) is the impulse response; j=√−1; ω is angular frequency in rad/s.

blocks.text: H(ω) is complex at each ω. Its magnitude |H(ω)| is amplitude gain. Its angle ∠H(ω) is phase shift.

blocks.where: A is input amplitude in volts or another unit; ω₀ is input angular frequency in rad/s; φ is input phase in radians or degrees; y(t) is the steady-state output.

items: Evaluate H(ω) at the input frequency ω₀.
Multiply the input amplitude A by |H(ω₀)|.
Add ∠H(ω₀) to the input phase φ.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this frequency-domain system analysis. It gives the steady-state sinusoidal output directly, without solving a differential equation in time.
Use h(t) when it is known. Integrate h(t)e^{−jωt} from −∞ to ∞. The result is a function of ω, not a single number.
Use the differential equation when it is known. For a constant-coefficient linear ordinary differential equation, replace d/dt by jω.

blocks.where: y′ is dy/dt; a and b are real constants; y(t) is output; x(t) is input; j=√−1; ω is angular frequency in rad/s.

blocks.text: For the RC low-pass, the equation is y′(t)+(1/RC)y(t)=(1/RC)x(t). Its frequency response is H(ω)=1/(1+jωRC). Here R is resistance in ohms, C is capacitance in farads, and RC is the time constant in seconds.
Do not confuse H(ω) with h(t). H(ω) is a complex gain at each frequency. h(t) is the time-domain impulse response. They are a Fourier-transform pair.
A magnitude sketch plots |H(ω)| against ω on linear axes. A phase sketch plots ∠H(ω). The figure shows one RC low-pass on linear axes.
Low-pass: |H(0)|=1 and |H| falls as ω rises. High-pass: |H(0)|=0 and |H| rises as ω rises. Band-pass: |H| peaks near a centre frequency and is small on both sides.
Read the output at the input frequency only. A low-pass does not remove all high frequencies; it attenuates them by the factor |H(ω)| and shifts them by ∠H(ω).
For distortionless transmission, |H(ω)| must be constant and ∠H(ω) must be linear in ω. See 3.6 for ideal filters and realizability.

figure.caption: The RC low-pass magnitude is 1 at zero frequency and falls to 0.707 at ω=1000 rad/s. The curve uses linear axes, so the drop is seen directly as a value, not as a logarithmic slope.

spec.aria: The RC low-pass magnitude is 1 at zero frequency and falls to 0.707 at ω=1000 rad/s.

examples.question: An RC low-pass filter has R=1 kΩ and C=1 μF. (a) Find H(ω). (b) For input x(t)=5 cos(1000t) V, find the steady-state output y(t).
steps: Compute the time constant: RC=1000 Ω × 1×10⁻⁶ F = 1×10⁻³ s.
At the input frequency ω₀=1000 rad/s, ω₀RC=1000×0.001=1.
Input amplitude A=5 V and input phase φ=0. Output amplitude=5×0.707=3.535 V≈3.54 V. Output phase=0−45°=−45°.
examples.check:
import math
R=1000.0
C=1e-6
w=1000.0
tau=R*C
H=1/(1+1j*w*tau)
mag=abs(H)
phase=math.degrees(math.atan2(H.imag,H.real))
amp=5*mag
print(f'{tau:.3f}')
print(f'{mag:.3f}')
print(f'{phase:.0f}')
print(f'{amp:.2f}')

traps: Treating H(ω) as h(t). H(ω) is complex frequency gain; h(t) is the time-domain impulse response.
Using only |H(ω)| for a sinusoidal input. The phase ∠H(ω) must also be added to the input phase.
Forgetting units of ω. Use rad/s. If a frequency f is given in Hz, first compute ω=2πf.
Adding |H| to the amplitude instead of multiplying. The output amplitude is A|H(ω₀)|.
Confusing low-pass and high-pass from memory. Check H(0): low-pass has |H(0)|=1; high-pass has |H(0)|=0.

quiz.q: Define the frequency response H(ω) of an LTI system.
quiz.a: H(ω)=Y(ω)/X(ω)=∫h(t)e^{−jωt}dt. It is the Fourier transform of the impulse response h(t).

quiz.q: Why does convolution in time become multiplication in frequency for an LTI system?
quiz.a: The Fourier transform of x(t)*h(t) is X(ω)H(ω). So the system multiplies each frequency component of the input by H(ω).

quiz.q: A system has H(ω)=1/(1+jω/1000). Input x(t)=2 cos(500t) V. Find the steady-state output y(t).
A system obeys y′(t)+2000y(t)=2000x(t). Find H(ω).
quiz.a: Replace d/dt by jω: (jω+2000)Y(ω)=2000X(ω). So H(ω)=2000/(jω+2000).

quiz.q: A system has |H(ω)|=1 for all ω and ∠H(ω)=−ωt₀. What does it do to any input?
quiz.a: It passes all frequencies with unit gain and delays every component by t₀. It is an ideal all-pass delay with linear phase and distortionless magnitude.

quiz.q: In the RC example, what is wrong with saying the output is 3.54 cos(1000t) V?
quiz.a: It ignores phase. The correct output is 3.54 cos(1000t−45°) V. The filter shifts the sinusoid by −45°.
h(t) is the time-domain impulse response. H(ω) is its Fourier transform: a complex frequency-domain gain and phase.

beyond: Not for the exam. Frequency response is the language of RF filters, audio equalizers, control loops and communication receivers. In practice engineers plot |H| and ∠H on logarithmic frequency axes, called Bode plots, and measure them with network analyzers. Software such as SPICE, MATLAB and Python's scipy.signal computes H from circuit or system models. Search next for Bode plots, transfer function and filter design.
